resources.title: mgcv: Mixed GAM Computation Vehicle with Automatic Smoothness Estimation
Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

sample_claims.text: Every input to the readmission risk model acts through a single plotted curve, so a clinician can read off how predicted risk changes with each input without running a separate explanation method.
The direction of each applicant attribute's effect in the credit model, as plotted with its confidence band, matches what credit risk specialists expect, and any departure has been explained.
The resource allocation model's score for any case is a baseline plus one contribution per policy factor, so each factor's share of a decision can be stated and audited.
Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.

techniques.name: Neuron Activation Analysis
techniques.description: Neuron activation analysis examines when individual neurons in a neural network respond strongly. The analyst runs a set of inputs through the model, finds the inputs that activate a chosen neuron most and least, and looks for the concept that separates them, such as buildings in an image classifier or French text in a language model. Some methods test the match automatically, for example by scoring how closely a neuron's activation lines up with labelled examples of a concept. The result is a list of neurons with candidate meanings and the evidence behind each. These meanings are correlations between inputs and activations, so they show what a neuron responds to, not what it does to the model's output.

example_use_cases.description: An ML team inspects a scene classifier trained to sort building and street images. For each neuron in a late layer they compare the images that activate it most with those that do not, using object labels from the dataset. Some neurons line up with a clear concept such as a building and others only weakly, which tells the team how much of the layer can be read.

A hospital assurance team examines a clinical language model and finds neurons whose strongest activations come from text about a particular drug class or condition. A clinician reviews whether the concepts are the expected ones. The finding shows which clinical concepts the model represents internally, not that these neurons cause any particular suggestion.

limitations.description: Many neurons respond to several unrelated concepts, or play different roles depending on the surrounding input. A single label such as 'toxic language' can then be wrong or only part of the story, and consistent interpretation across scenarios is hard.

Behaviour is often spread across many neurons instead of held in one, so a neuron-by-neuron view can miss it. Checking combinations of neurons is much harder than checking single ones, and the number of combinations grows quickly.

The analysis shows which inputs make a neuron fire, not what the neuron contributes to the output. Showing that a neuron matters needs a separate experiment that switches it off or alters it and measures the effect.

A neuron can only be matched to concepts the analyst has examples for. In image models this means a densely labelled dataset, and a neuron whose concept is missing from it goes unexplained or is mislabelled.

The method needs access to the model's internal activations, so it cannot be used on a model reached only through an API. Large language models have hundreds of thousands of neurons or more, so in practice only a chosen subset can be examined and labelled with care.

resources.title: On the Value of Labeled Data and Symbolic Methods for Hidden Neuron Activation Analysis
resources.abstract: A major challenge in Explainable AI is in correctly interpreting activations of hidden neurons: accurate interpretations would help answer the question of what a deep learning system internally detects as relevant in the input, demystifying the otherwise black-box nature of deep learning systems. The state of the art indicates that hidden node activations can, in some cases, be interpretable in a way that makes sense to humans, but systematic automated methods that would be able to hypothesize and verify interpretations of hidden neuron activations are underexplored. This is particularly the case for approaches that can both draw explanations from substantial background knowledge, and that are based on inherently explainable (symbolic) methods.   In this paper, we introduce a novel model-agnostic post-hoc Explainable AI method demonstrating that it provides meaningful interpretations. Our approach is based on using a Wikipedia-derived concept hierarchy with approximately 2 million classes as background knowledge, and utilizes OWL-reasoning-based Concept Induction for explanation generation. Additionally, we explore and compare the capabilities of off-the-shelf pre-trained multimodal-based explainable methods.   Our results indicate that our approach can automatically attach meaningful class expressions as explanations to individual neurons in the dense layer of a Convolutional Neural Network. Evaluation through statistical analysis and degree of concept activation in the hidden layer show that our method provides a competitive edge in both quantitative and qualitative aspects compared to prior work.

resources.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
resources.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
resources.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

sample_claims.text: For each sampled neuron in the clinical language model, the concept that best explains its strongest activations is recorded with a match score, and neurons below the agreed score are reported as not interpreted.
The concept labels assigned to the classifier's late-layer neurons hold on held-out images: the labelled neurons activate far more strongly on images of the concept than on images without it.
The language-model analysis documents the contexts producing high and low activation for each selected unit.

techniques.name: Causal Mediation Analysis in Language Models
techniques.description: Causal mediation analysis traces which internal components of a language model carry the effect of a change in the input to the output. The analyst makes a controlled change to the input, such as swapping 'nurse' for 'man' in a prompt, and measures how the model's next-word probabilities shift. To find the indirect effect through one component (a single neuron, or an attention head, which is the part of the model that chooses which earlier words to focus on), they feed the model the original input but give that component the value it took on the changed input. To find the direct effect, they feed the changed input but hold that component at its original value. Repeating this across many components shows where in the network a behaviour is carried.

example_use_cases.description: A safety team finds that a language model gives unsafe medical advice when a request is phrased as an instruction rather than a question. They compare outputs for the two phrasings and use mediation analysis to find which attention heads carry most of the shift in the probability of the unsafe reply, so a fix can target those heads and the analysis can be rerun to check it worked.

A research team studying why a language model sometimes gets subject-verb agreement wrong in sentences with an intervening clause changes the number of the subject noun and measures the shift in the verb's probability. Mediation analysis then shows which neurons carry the number information, and whether the same neurons are used across sentence structures.

limitations.description: Needs white-box access and knowledge of the architecture. The analyst must read and overwrite activations at chosen points inside the model, so it cannot be used on a model offered only through an API, and a poorly chosen intervention point can give misleading conclusions.

Conclusions hold for the contrast tested. Swapping 'nurse' for 'man' and tracking one probability ratio tests a single contrast, and a different prompt set or outcome measure can point to different components. Effects also differ between models: larger GPT-2 models showed larger effects, and masked language models matched less well.

Every component and every prompt needs its own forward passes, so testing all the neurons or heads of a large model on many prompts is expensive. Analysts often test a subset or groups of components, which can miss effects elsewhere in the network.

Single-component effects do not simply add up. Vig et al. found that intervening on all neurons together produced an effect far larger than the sum of the single-neuron effects, so ranking components one at a time can understate or misplace where a behaviour is carried.

The split into direct and indirect effects is not guaranteed to be exact. In a non-linear network the total effect need not equal their sum, and Vig et al. report only an approximate match for GPT-2, so the split should be checked rather than assumed.

resources.title: Investigating Gender Bias in Language Models Using Causal Mediation Analysis
resources.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

resources.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language Models
resources.abstract: Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate the magnitude of models’ preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across architectures and model sizes—notably, that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

techniques.name: Concept Activation Vectors
techniques.description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

resources.title: FastCAV: Efficient Computation of Concept Activation Vectors for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Concepts such as objects, patterns, and shapes are how humans understand the world. Building on this intuition, concept-based explainability methods aim to study representations learned by deep neural networks in relation to human-understandable concepts. Here, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) are an important tool and can identify whether a model learned a concept or not. However, the computational cost and time requirements of existing CAV computation pose a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale, high-dimensional architectures. To address this limitation, we introduce FastCAV, a novel approach that accelerates the extraction of CAVs by up to 63.6x (on average 46.4x). We provide a theoretical foundation for our approach and give concrete assumptions under which it is equivalent to established SVM-based methods. Our empirical results demonstrate that CAVs calculated with FastCAV maintain similar performance while being more efficient and stable. In downstream applications, i.e., concept-based explanation methods, we show that FastCAV can act as a replacement leading to equivalent insights. Hence, our approach enables previously infeasible investigations of deep models, which we demonstrate by tracking the evolution of concepts during model training.

resources.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
resources.abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.

resources.title: Global and Local Interpretability for Cardiac MRI Classification
resources.abstract: Deep learning methods for classifying medical images have demonstrated impressive accuracy in a wide range of tasks but often these models are hard to interpret, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. In this work we introduce a convolutional neural network model for identifying disease in temporal sequences of cardiac MR segmentations which is interpretable in terms of clinically familiar measurements. The model is based around a variational autoencoder, reducing the input into a low-dimensional latent space in which classification occurs. We then use the recently developed `concept activation vector' technique to associate concepts which are diagnostically meaningful (eg. clinical biomarkers such as `low left-ventricular ejection fraction') to certain vectors in the latent space. These concepts are then qualitatively inspected by observing the change in the image domain resulting from interpolations in the latent space in the direction of these vectors. As a result, when the model classifies images it is also capable of providing naturally interpretable concepts relevant to that classification and demonstrating the meaning of those concepts in the image domain. Our approach is demonstrated on the UK Biobank cardiac MRI dataset where we detect the presence of coronary artery disease.

resources.title: Concept attribution: Explaining CNN decisions to physicians
resources.abstract: Deep learning explainability is often reached by gradient-based approaches that attribute the network output to perturbations of the input pixels. However, the relevance of input pixels may be difficult to relate to relevant image features in some applications, e.g. diagnostic measures in medical imaging. The framework described in this paper shifts the attribution focus from pixel values to user-defined concepts. By checking if certain diagnostic measures are present in the learned representations, experts can explain and entrust the network output. Being post-hoc, our method does not alter the network training and can be easily plugged into the latest state-of-the-art convolutional networks. This paper presents the main components of the framework for attribution to concepts, in addition to the introduction of a spatial pooling operation on top of the feature maps to obtain a solid interpretability analysis. Furthermore, regularized regression is analyzed as a solution to the regression overfitting in high-dimensionality latent spaces. The versatility of the proposed approach is shown by experiments on two medical applications, namely histopathology and retinopathy, and on one non-medical task, the task of handwritten digit classification. The obtained explanations are in line with clinicians' guidelines and complementary to widely used visualization tools such as saliency maps.

sample_claims.text: The chest X-ray classifier's 'pneumonia' predictions are significantly sensitive to clinically recognised findings and not significantly sensitive to scanner type or patient positioning, at the layers tested.

The content-tagging classifier's TCAV scores for the ethnicity and gender concept sets are recorded for every output class at the tested layers, and the classes with significant sensitivity are listed for review.
The traffic-sign classifier's sensitivity to graffiti, snow cover and glare concepts is documented with significance-tested TCAV scores for each sign class the approval authority has requested.
The object recogniser's class predictions depend mainly on concepts that domain experts regard as meaningful for that class, such as shape and texture, rather than on background concepts.

techniques.name: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Evaluation
techniques.description: Chain-of-thought faithfulness evaluation tests whether the step-by-step reasoning a language model writes out is what actually produces its answer, rather than an account added afterwards. One set of tests alters the reasoning itself, by cutting it short, inserting a deliberate mistake, rewording it or replacing it with filler text, and checks whether the final answer changes. If the answer never changes, the reasoning is probably not doing the work. Another set adds a cue to the input that points to a particular answer, such as a user's stated guess, and checks whether the answer shifts while the explanation never mentions the cue. Each test gives a rate, such as how often the answer changes, and passing one rules out a single kind of unfaithfulness without showing that the reasoning is faithful or that its steps are correct.

example_use_cases.description: An education company's tutoring assistant shows pupils its step-by-step working beside each answer to a science question. Before telling pupils that the working explains the answer, the evaluation team cuts the working short and inserts a deliberate mistake on a test set, and records how often the final answer changes. Where it rarely does, as Lanham et al. found for grade-school science sets, the working is shown as an illustration, not as the reason.

A lender's model-validation team lets an underwriting assistant write a rationale for each recommendation that staff keep on file. It reruns validation cases with a line added saying a senior colleague favours approval. Where the recommendation moves towards the line but the rationale never mentions it, as Turpin et al. found for suggested answers, the rationale is not accepted as the record of why the case was decided.

A public body choosing between two sizes of one language-model family for a casework summarising tool wants staff to rely on the reasoning the model shows. On multiple-choice questions built from its own case files, it records how often each model's answer changes when its reasoning is removed, shuffling answer order to control for letter preference as Bentham et al. did, and prefers the model whose answers depend on its reasoning.

A recruitment platform's audit team uses a language model to compare two candidates for shortlisting when the evidence for each is thin. Following the social-bias test in Turpin et al., it submits each pair twice with the weak evidence swapped between the candidates and counts pairs where the same candidate is picked both times. Those pairs show evidence weighed inconsistently, so the reasoning is not accepted as showing what drove the choice.

limitations.description: Passing does not show faithfulness. Each test rules out one way the reasoning could be unfaithful, and the authors call the tests necessary but not sufficient. There is no independent view of the model's actual process to check against, so a clean result supports a narrower claim than 'the reasoning is faithful'.

Results do not carry over between models or tasks. Lanham et al. found that the reasoning changed the final answer under 10% of the time on three science question sets but over 60% on algebra word problems, and that faithfulness varied with model size. Re-measure for the model version and task type that will be deployed.

The answer-change score can reflect something other than faithfulness. Bentham et al. repeated Lanham et al.'s measure on three other model families. After correcting for a model's habit of favouring certain answer letters, apparent unfaithfulness in weaker models fell sharply, and the corrected score tracked accuracy (R-squared of 0.74).

Input-cue tests find only the influences the evaluator thinks to add. Turpin et al. tried three cues, and say their setup only tests faithfulness against minor changes to the input. A model that passes can still be swayed by a cue nobody tried, and the cue must point to a wrong answer to show up as an accuracy drop.

The tests are costly and need control of generation. Lanham et al. sampled 100 reasoning chains per question and re-queried after each truncation; Turpin et al. subsampled for cost. Inserted mistakes were judged plausible in at least 80% of cases, so up to a fifth may test nothing, and Bentham et al. note the procedure needs manual intervention in decoding.

resources.title: cot-unfaithfulness (code for Turpin et al. 2023)
Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve strong performance on many tasks by producing step-by-step reasoning before giving a final output, often referred to as chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT). It is tempting to interpret these CoT explanations as the LLM's process for solving a task. This level of transparency into LLMs' predictions would yield significant safety benefits. However, we find that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. We demonstrate that CoT explanations can be heavily influenced by adding biasing features to model inputs--e.g., by reordering the multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to make the answer always "(A)"--which models systematically fail to mention in their explanations. When we bias models toward incorrect answers, they frequently generate CoT explanations rationalizing those answers. This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard, when testing with GPT-3.5 from OpenAI and Claude 1.0 from Anthropic. On a social-bias task, model explanations justify giving answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of these social biases. Our findings indicate that CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading, which risks increasing our trust in LLMs without guaranteeing their safety. Building more transparent and explainable systems will require either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.

resources.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

resources.title: Chain-of-Thought Unfaithfulness as Disguised Accuracy
resources.abstract: Understanding the extent to which Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generations align with a large language model's (LLM) internal computations is critical for deciding whether to trust an LLM's output. As a proxy for CoT faithfulness, Lanham et al. (2023) propose a metric that measures a model's dependence on its CoT for producing an answer. Within a single family of proprietary models, they find that LLMs exhibit a scaling-then-inverse-scaling relationship between model size and their measure of faithfulness, and that a 13 billion parameter model exhibits increased faithfulness compared to models ranging from 810 million to 175 billion parameters in size. We evaluate whether these results generalize as a property of all LLMs. We replicate the experimental setup in their section focused on scaling experiments with three different families of models and, under specific conditions, successfully reproduce the scaling trends for CoT faithfulness they report. However, after normalizing the metric to account for a model's bias toward certain answer choices, unfaithfulness drops significantly for smaller less-capable models. This normalized faithfulness metric is also strongly correlated ($R^2$=0.74) with accuracy, raising doubts about its validity for evaluating faithfulness.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
techniques.description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer shows its fraud analysts a feature attribution beside each held transaction and needs it within the two seconds before the review queue refreshes. Benchmarking on the production server at peak queue load, it finds that a sampling-based explainer misses the budget for about one explanation in twenty while an explainer specific to its tree ensemble stays well inside it, and adopts the second once its attributions pass the same faithfulness tests.

A hospital adding an explanation panel to a sepsis-risk alert in its electronic health record agrees with clinicians that the panel must load within one second of a nurse opening the alert. The informatics team times explanations on the hospital's own servers with a week of real alerts at typical volume, reports the 95th percentile and the slowest case against that limit, and repeats the measurement after each model or software update.

An online marketplace shows each seller the main reasons its moderation model held a new listing for review, and the page must update within three seconds. Before launch, the team times the service on its production servers with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace; the first request after each quiet period is far slower because the explainer and its background data load on demand. It keeps a loaded explainer running, re-measures, and reports the slowest case.

limitations.description: Speed and explanation quality trade off through the explainer's settings. Sampling-based explainers run faster with fewer samples or a smaller background dataset, but SHAP's documentation notes that more samples give lower-variance estimates, so a faster setting gives noisier explanations. A latency result holds only for the settings tested, and must be measured at the settings whose faithfulness and stability were checked, or a configuration may meet the budget with untested explanations.

Times depend on the hardware, the implementation and the load at the moment of measurement, which Canha et al. single out as the main caveat on their speed metric, so a figure from a developer's workstation does not carry over to a shared production server or an edge device. Any change to the model, the explainer version, the hardware or the traffic pattern calls for re-measurement, and the configuration must be recorded with the result for it to be checked or repeated.

Claims about the slowest cases need many timed explanations. MLPerf Inference, which sets tail-latency bounds for model inference in the same way, sizes its runs so that a 99th-percentile bound holds with 99 per cent confidence, which at its chosen margin takes about 263,000 queries. A few hundred timings can support a claim about the median but not about the 99th percentile, and a single timed run supports neither.

A fast explanation is not necessarily a good one. Latency says nothing about whether an explanation reflects what the model did or whether people can use it, and it leaves out the time a person needs to read it. It supports a claim about explanations only alongside tests of faithfulness and stability and, where people act on the explanations, a study of whether they can use them within the time available.

The budget has to come from the decision, not from a generic scale. Canha et al.'s cut-offs reflect general limits on human response time, which may be looser or tighter than a particular workflow allows, and a budget that leaves out the time to run the model, move the data and display the result will be met in the benchmark and missed in use; MLPerf likewise derives its server-scenario latency bounds from the user's overall time target.

techniques.name: Deletion and Insertion Curves
techniques.description: Deletion and insertion curves test whether a feature-attribution explanation, such as a heatmap over an image or highlighted words in a text, puts first the input features the model actually relies on. For the deletion curve, the evaluator removes features in the order the explanation ranks them, most important first, replacing each with a neutral value such as zero, the dataset mean, random noise or a blurred copy, and records the model's score for the explained class after each step; a faithful ranking makes the score fall quickly, so a smaller area under the curve is better (equivalently, a larger area over it, the AOPC score Samek et al. report). The insertion curve runs the other way: it starts from an input with every feature removed or blurred, restores features in ranked order, and rewards a fast rise. For text, the same procedure is often reported as comprehensiveness (how far the predicted-class probability drops when the top-ranked words are deleted) and sufficiency (how far it drops when only those words are kept), either at one cut-off or averaged over cut-offs from the top 1% to the top 50% of words. Explanation methods are compared on the same model, inputs and replacement value, against a random ranking as a baseline, and the result shows how well the ranking tracks the model's behaviour, not whether the highlighted features make sense to a person.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's cardiology informatics team has a deep network that measures intervals and amplitudes from 12-lead ECGs and must choose which heatmap method to show cardiologists. It perturbs the highest-ranked sample points first, one per step, tracks the rise in measurement error over several thousand ECGs, and compares each method's area under the error curve with that of random heatmaps. Because expert preferences and the curves can disagree, it reports both before choosing.

A regulator's data team routes consumer complaints with a fine-tuned transformer classifier and wants to highlight for caseworkers the words behind each routing decision. Before choosing between two word-attribution methods, it computes comprehensiveness and sufficiency on a validation sample at the 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50% cut-offs and adopts a method only if it clearly beats randomly ranked words on both measures.

A rail operator's engineering team uses an image classifier to flag defects in track inspection photographs and wants heatmaps that point inspectors to the defect. It runs deletion with pixels set to a constant and insertion from a blurred image for three heatmap methods, then repeats the deletion run with a second replacement value, and adopts a method only if it ranks first under both.

limitations.description: Removing pixels or words produces inputs unlike anything the model was trained on, so part of the drop in score can be the model reacting to an unfamiliar input rather than to the loss of the information the explanation pointed to, and the shape of the removed region can itself carry class information. Results are least trustworthy when large parts of the input are removed; variants that retrain the model or fill removed pixels from their neighbours reduce the effect.

The score depends on how features are removed and in what order. On one image classifier, the best-ranked method changed when removed pixels were set to the dataset mean instead of random colours, removing the least relevant pixels first ranked the methods roughly in reverse of removing the most relevant first, and rankings varied from image to image. A comparison holds only for the stated replacement value, order, step size and fraction removed, and should be checked under a second replacement.

Only the order of the attribution scores counts, not their size, so explanations with very different magnitudes can receive the same score. Taking absolute values of signed attributions changes the order and hence the result. The curves cannot tell an explanation that ranks the right features but gives them misleading magnitudes from one that gets both right; that needs a measure that uses the attribution values.

The curves show whether the ranking tracks the model, not whether the explanation is useful or correct for the domain: a model that relies on a spurious cue receives a faithful explanation of that cue. In a study of ECG models, ECG experts' choice of the best heatmap method disagreed considerably with the perturbation ranking, so a good curve does not show that experts will find the explanation helpful.

Each curve needs one model evaluation per step, for every input and method compared, so fine-grained curves over large images, long documents or big test sets are expensive. In the original region-perturbation study, two settings over 5,040 images each, with 100 steps repeated ten times because the replacement values were random, took roughly 36 hours on a workstation with 20 hyper-threaded Xeon cores in 2015. Coarser steps cut the cost but make the curve less able to separate methods.

techniques.name: Explanation Infidelity
techniques.description: Explanation infidelity scores a feature-attribution explanation (one importance score per input feature) by how well it predicts what the model does when the input is changed. The evaluator chooses a distribution of meaningful perturbations, for example small random noise around a reference input, or setting random subsets of features or square patches of an image to a reference value, and draws many perturbations from it. For each one it compares the change in output that the explanation predicts, the sum over features of each feature's perturbation multiplied by its attribution score, with the change the model actually shows, its output on the original input minus its output on the perturbed one. Infidelity is the average squared difference between the two, estimated by random sampling, so lower is better; Yeh et al. (2019), who proposed it, showed that several common explanation methods each have the lowest infidelity for one particular perturbation distribution, so the distribution chosen defines what counts as faithful in a given test. Scores are averaged over a set of inputs and compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, under the same perturbations; unlike a deletion curve, the score uses the size of each attribution as well as its rank.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team must choose which attribution method supplies the reason scores shown to credit analysts for a neural-network default model. It computes infidelity on held-out applications for three candidate methods, with perturbations that set random subsets of features to a documented reference applicant and with rescaling switched on, and records the perturbation distribution in the validation report beside the method it selects.

A manufacturer's quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defects in weld radiographs and smooths its gradient heatmaps by averaging them over noisy copies of each image. It sets the amount of noise by computing infidelity under square-patch perturbations sized to typical defects on validation radiographs and choosing the level with the lowest score, since in the original study infidelity first fell and then rose as smoothing increased.

A hospital's clinical AI team retrains its deterioration-risk model each quarter and shows ward staff the attribution scores behind each alert. After every retraining it recomputes rescaled infidelity on the latest validation data, with the perturbations fixed at first validation, for the deployed attribution settings and two alternatives, and holds the release for review if the deployed settings are no longer the lowest, since the absolute score also moves with the retrained model.

limitations.description: What counts as faithful is set by the perturbation distribution. Yeh et al. show that several common explanations each have the lowest possible infidelity for one particular distribution (for example, Shapley values for the feature-subset scheme that SHAP uses), so a comparison can be won by choosing matching perturbations. The distribution should be fixed in advance and justified by the question the explanation is meant to answer.

The score is a squared error between predicted and actual changes in output, so it depends on the scale of the attribution scores: two methods that rank features identically but on different scales get different infidelity. Yeh et al. rescale each explanation optimally before scoring, and Captum offers this rescaling as an option that is off by default; without it, comparisons across methods mislead.

Some attribution methods multiply each feature's sensitivity by the input's distance from a reference and others do not, and the perturbation term has to be computed to match. Yeh et al. compare the two kinds separately, and Captum asks the user to state which kind is being scored; getting this wrong produces a score that reflects the mismatch rather than the explanation.

It follows from the definition, though Yeh et al. do not discuss it, that the predicted change is a sum of per-feature effects. Where the model's response to the chosen perturbations is not additive, as when pixels within an object or words within a phrase interact, no attribution can reach zero infidelity. The floor is the same for every method scored on the same model and perturbations, so rankings stand, but the score is not the explanation's error alone and cannot be compared across models.

The score is an average over random perturbations, each needing a model evaluation. Yeh et al. used 1,000 perturbations per input; Captum's default is 10. Few samples give noisy scores, so small differences between methods need repeated runs, while many samples multiply the cost by the inputs, methods and settings compared. Quantus's built-in version perturbs square patches and so handles image data only.

resources.title: On the (In)fidelity and Sensitivity of Explanations
resources.abstract: We consider objective evaluation measures of saliency explanations for complex black-box machine learning models. We propose simple robust variants of two notions that have been considered in recent literature: (in)fidelity, and sensitivity. We analyze optimal explanations with respect to both these measures, and while the optimal explanation for sensitivity is a vacuous constant explanation, the optimal explanation for infidelity is a novel combination of two popular explanation methods. By varying the perturbation distribution that defines infidelity, we obtain novel explanations by optimizing infidelity, which we show to out-perform existing explanations in both quantitative and qualitative measurements. Another salient question given these measures is how to modify any given explanation to have better values with respect to these measures. We propose a simple modification based on lowering sensitivity, and moreover show that when done appropriately, we could simultaneously improve both sensitivity as well as fidelity.

techniques.name: Explanation Max-Sensitivity
techniques.description: Explanation max-sensitivity measures how stable an explanation is: whether inputs that differ only slightly, in ways that should not change the answer, receive very different explanations. For each input, the evaluator samples many nearby points within a small radius (for example, no feature moved by more than 0.02 on a 0 to 1 scale), recomputes the explanation at each with the same explanation method, and records the largest distance between a recomputed explanation and the original; Yeh et al. (2019) defined the measure and estimated it by random sampling. Dividing each change in the explanation by the distance the input moved, and taking the largest ratio, gives the closely related local Lipschitz estimate of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), which they maximised with an optimiser rather than by sampling; the two are not interchangeable, because the ratio is dominated by the smallest input changes and can be unbounded where max-sensitivity is finite, so they can rank methods differently. Lower scores mean a more stable explanation, and scores are compared across explanation methods, or across settings of one method, on the same inputs, radius and distance measure. The test treats the explanation method as a black box, so it applies to attribution scores from any method, but on its own it says nothing about faithfulness: a constant explanation that ignores the model is perfectly stable.

example_use_cases.description: A consumer lender tells declined applicants the main reasons for each decision, taken from Shapley-value attributions of its credit model. Its model-risk team measures max-sensitivity on a sample of declined applications, perturbing features only within bounds the lending policy treats as immaterial, to choose between two sampling budgets for the explainer, because applicants who differ trivially should not be given different main reasons.

An Earth-observation team comparing attribution methods for a multi-label land-cover classifier on satellite image patches computes max-sensitivity for each method together with a most-relevant-first deletion curve, and short-lists methods that do well on both. Pairing the two matters because smoothing an explanation lowers its sensitivity, and a stable method is worth choosing only if it also tracks the model.

A vehicle perception team averages gradient heatmaps over noisy copies of each camera frame to steady them for safety reviewers. It sets the noise level by tracking max-sensitivity and infidelity together on validation frames as the level rises, and picks the point where sensitivity has levelled off before infidelity starts to increase, since too much smoothing produces stable maps that no longer reflect the detector.

limitations.description: A low score does not mean the explanation is right. The most stable explanation possible is a constant one that ignores the model, and heavy smoothing keeps lowering sensitivity while eventually making the explanation less faithful. Max-sensitivity should be reported with a measure of faithfulness on the same inputs, and a method should not be chosen for stability alone.

The sampled maximum is a lower bound on the true worst case: with a handful of random samples per input (Captum's default is 10), the largest change found can be far below the largest that exists. Deliberately chosen perturbations that leave the prediction unchanged can alter explanations dramatically, so a low score does not show that explanations resist manipulation.

The number depends on settings that differ between tools: the radius, the distance measure for inputs and explanations, the number of samples and whether explanations are normalised first. By default Captum samples 10 points within a radius of 0.02 and Quantus 200 points within 0.2, ten times wider, while Yeh et al. used 50 points within 0.1 and normalised explanations to unit length. Scores are comparable only under identical settings and identically scaled inputs.

A high score can come from the model rather than the explanation method. Near a decision boundary, or where the model's output changes quickly, a faithful explanation should change, and Yeh et al. note that explanations built from the model's own sensitivity can be more sensitive than the model. Perturbations that change the prediction should be excluded or reported separately.

The test assumes inputs can be nudged by small continuous amounts. For words, categories or other discrete inputs no such small change exists, and the fallback of comparing explanations of similar examples already in the test data is weaker and depends on how many close neighbours the data contain. The per-unit Lipschitz form can be unbounded for gradient explanations of ReLU networks, one reason Yeh et al. prefer the undivided maximum, which stays finite.

resources.abstract: We argue that robustness of explanations---i.e., that similar inputs should give rise to similar explanations---is a key desideratum for interpretability. We introduce metrics to quantify robustness and demonstrate that current methods do not perform well according to these metrics. Finally, we propose ways that robustness can be enforced on existing interpretability approaches.
