techniques.name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
techniques.description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology AI group considering saliency maps as a guide to where a chest-radiograph model sees a pneumothorax runs cascading randomisation on the trained network, measuring structural similarity between original and randomised maps after each block. It sets aside methods whose maps stay similar, as several common methods did in a published study of this task, unless a deletion test shows they still track the model, and uses the rest only alongside a separately validated localisation model.

An insurer's fraud analytics team shows investigators attribution scores for each claim flagged by a neural-network model. Before rollout it runs independent layer randomisation, one layer at a time, and checks that rank correlation without absolute values falls for every layer, so that the scores investigators see depend on the trained weights throughout the network rather than mostly on the claim's raw feature values.

A wind-farm operator's reliability team uses a one-dimensional convolutional network on gearbox vibration signals and gives maintenance engineers heatmaps over each signal. It runs the data randomisation test by training the same architecture on shuffled fault labels until it fits them, and keeps only heatmap methods whose maps differ clearly between the two networks, since a map that survives shuffled labels cannot show what the network learned about faults.

limitations.description: Passing is easy for an explanation that carries no information. Binder et al. show that attribution maps with no correlation between neighbouring pixels score well in model randomisation tests, and that top-down randomisation tends to preserve the scale of forward-pass activations, so even a good explanation can change only so much. They argue the test should not alone decide whether a method is kept: two methods that score poorly on it beat several gradient methods in occlusion-based tests.

The verdict depends on how similarity is measured. In the original study, rank correlation with absolute values and structural similarity stayed high for some methods after randomisation while rank correlation without absolute values fell to near zero, because randomisation flipped signs but kept the input's outline. There is no agreed pass threshold and libraries set their own defaults, so the measure, absolute-value setting and threshold must be reported with the result.

The similarity measures are sensitive to noise, so a method with noisy maps looks changed by randomisation partly because of its own noise, and its score is overstated. Later work proposes repairs: averaging each explanation over noisy copies of the input before comparing (Smooth MPRT), or comparing how much more complex the explanation becomes after full randomisation (Efficient MPRT); its authors report more reliable results with both.

The model parameter test needs the weights and a layered network, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an interface. The data randomisation test needs the training data and pipeline and a network able to memorise shuffled labels; the original study trained to over 95% training accuracy, which for a large model costs a full training run.

Most evidence for the tests comes from image classifiers. Passing says nothing about whether the highlighted regions match what matters in the domain: in a chest-radiograph study, every saliency method, including those that passed the randomisation test, localised abnormalities worse than a dedicated detection or segmentation network.

resources.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
resources.abstract:
Saliency methods have emerged as a popular tool to highlight features in an input
deemed relevant for the prediction of a learned model. Several saliency methods
have been proposed, often guided by visual appeal on image data. In this work, we
propose an actionable methodology to evaluate what kinds of explanations a given
method can and cannot provide. We find that reliance, solely, on visual assessment
can be misleading. Through extensive experiments we show that some existing
saliency methods are independent both of the model and of the data generating
process. Consequently, methods that fail the proposed tests are inadequate for
tasks that are sensitive to either data or model, such as, finding outliers in the data,
explaining the relationship between inputs and outputs that the model learned,
and debugging the model. We interpret our findings through an analogy with
edge detection in images, a technique that requires neither training data nor model.
Theory in the case of a linear model and a single-layer convolutional neural network
supports our experimental findings.

Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

techniques.name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
techniques.description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.

techniques.name: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Analysis
techniques.description: Sparse autoencoder feature analysis looks for human-interpretable units inside a neural network, usually a language model, by learning from the activations at one layer a large dictionary of directions, called features, such that each activation vector can be rebuilt from only a few of them. Unlike neuron activation analysis it does not take the network's own neurons as the units, since single neurons often respond to several unrelated things, and unlike concept activation vectors it needs no labelled examples of a concept chosen in advance, because the features are found without supervision. The analyst records activations at the chosen layer over a large body of ordinary text and trains an autoencoder, a network with one hidden layer usually several times wider than the layer studied, to reconstruct them while a sparsity penalty keeps most hidden units at zero; the decoder weights of each hidden unit then give one feature direction. Each feature is labelled from the inputs on which it fires most strongly, by a person or by a language model that writes a description, which is then scored on how well it predicts the feature's activations on other text, and the label is tested by removing or amplifying the feature inside the running model and checking the change in output. The output is a catalogue of labelled features with example activations, interpretability scores and measured effects, plus a reconstruction score saying how much of the layer's behaviour the dictionary accounts for; the features can then serve as units for causal mediation analysis, which traces pathways, while this method finds and checks the units themselves.

example_use_cases.description: Before deploying an open-weights language model as a customer-service assistant, a bank's AI assurance team uses sparse autoencoders published for that model to find features active on prompts where the assistant should refuse to give investment advice. It tests each candidate by suppressing it and measuring the change in refusal rate, and records which labelled features the refusal behaviour depends on in the model's assurance file.

A bioinformatics group using a protein language model to annotate newly sequenced proteins trains sparse autoencoders on its embeddings and compares the features with database annotations of binding sites, structural motifs and domains. Features that match known biology are used to propose candidate annotations for curators to verify, features that fire widely with no clear meaning are flagged for review, and the model's own annotation accuracy is still tested on held-out proteins.

A team that fine-tuned a language model to triage clinical referral letters lists the sparse autoencoder features that most change the 'urgent' score on a validation set, and checks whether they describe clinical content or properties of the letter, such as the referring practice's template. A template feature among the leading drivers is recorded as a finding and leads to retraining on reformatted letters.

limitations.description: The dictionary does not capture everything the layer carries, and what it misses cannot be inspected. In the originating study, replacing one layer of a small language model with its reconstruction raised perplexity from 25 to 40; a concurrent study recovered 79% of a layer's contribution to the loss in its main run. Not finding a feature for a concept does not show that the model lacks it.

The features found are not unique. Larger dictionaries split a feature into narrower ones (one base64 feature at 512 features became three at 4,096), and for a 131,000-feature autoencoder on one layer of Llama 3 8B only about 30% of features were shared by two runs differing only in random seed. A conclusion resting on one feature should name the autoencoder used and be checked on a second run.

Labels are hypotheses drawn from the top-activating examples, and automated scores are modest: the first five features reported in the originating study scored between -0.11 and 0.57, and the advantage over simpler decompositions faded in later layers. Back a label with an intervention that changes the output as the label predicts before citing it as evidence.

It needs the model's internal activations, plus storage and compute to train an autoencoder for each layer studied (one concurrent study trained on 8 billion activation vectors from a single layer). For large models practitioners often rely on autoencoders released for particular open-weights models, so the method is not available for a model reached only through an API.

Being interpretable does not make the features better for a given task. In a 2025 study of detecting concepts from model activations, probes built on autoencoder features did not beat logistic regression on the raw activations on average, and the spurious correlations and data problems they exposed could also be found with simpler baselines. Where detection is the goal, compare against such baselines.

techniques.name: TimeSHAP
techniques.description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's fraud operations team runs TimeSHAP on each alert from its recurrent account-takeover model, so the analyst reviewing an alert sees which earlier events (for example a password change, then a login from a new device) and which features carried the score, not only the payment being held. The analyst uses this to decide whether to release the payment or contact the customer, and the model team samples the explanations to check that the drivers match known fraud patterns.

A hospital data-science team validating a recurrent model that predicts next-day escalation of treatment for patients in intensive care computes event- and feature-level TimeSHAP values for test-set patients and reviews them with clinicians. Drivers the clinicians judge implausible, such as an indicator that a measurement is missing outweighing the measurements themselves, are investigated before the model is used in a prospective study.

An airport's forecasting team using a recurrent model to warn of fog in the next six hours from the past 48 hours of station observations uses the pruning statistics and global event plots to find how far back the model actually draws on, and the feature attributions to check that humidity, temperature and wind lead each warning. The findings set the input window for the next retraining and go into the model's validation report.

limitations.description: Every attribution is measured against the background chosen to stand for a removed event or feature, the training-data average in the original paper. A sequence containing averaged events may be unlike anything the model has seen, and another background gives other attributions; the original authors note that a feature scoring zero for every sequence may reflect the background rather than the model. Report the background with the results.

Exact values need every combination of events, which doubles with each event. On the original fraud data (median sequence about 138 events), exact values were possible for only 10% of sequences with 32,000 sampled combinations, and repeated runs disagreed (relative standard deviation 1.71 without pruning, 0.98 at the chosen tolerance). With tens of thousands of model calls per explanation, explaining every scored event in real time is impractical; the alerts people review are the usual scope.

Pruning trades detail on older events for speed and stability. All events before the cut-off share one attribution. The cut-off test compares the older block's net, signed attribution with a user-set tolerance, so by construction an early event that pushed the score up can pass unseen if others pushed it down; the original paper does not measure how often this happens. Results change with the tolerance, so fix it in advance and report it.

It explains one score per sequence: the reference implementation expects the model to return a single value for each sequence. A model with many outputs, such as a forecast for several lead times or locations, needs a separate run or a chosen summary for each. The attributions show what the model relies on, not causes in the world: in the original study a high attribution to customer age led to a bias audit, which was needed to establish the disparity.

Each event and feature receives one number, so an effect that arises only from a combination, such as a settings change followed by a login from a new device, is shared out among its parts: an analyst sees each part with some credit but cannot tell that they matter only together. Cell-level values are computed only where the top-ranked events and features intersect. A clinical study using the method found escalation effects hard to see and suggested interactions as the cause.

techniques.name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
techniques.description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.

techniques.name: Explanation Satisfaction Scale
techniques.description: The Explanation Satisfaction Scale is a short questionnaire on which people who have used an AI system's explanations rate how satisfying and sufficient they found them; Hoffman, Mueller, Klein and Litman developed it in the DARPA Explainable AI programme to capture the user's judgement of an explanation, as distinct from a researcher's judgement of its quality. Each item is a statement about the explanation, for example that from it the user understands how the system works, or that it is satisfying, has sufficient detail, seems complete, tells the user how to use the system, is useful to their goals or shows how accurate the system is, and each is rated on a five-point scale from 'I agree strongly' to 'I disagree strongly'. Participants complete it after they have worked with the system and received explanations, usually once for each explanation condition in a study that compares conditions; the published form sets no scoring rule or threshold, and the implementation by one of its authors in the OpenScales library scores it as the mean of the item ratings. Versions differ: the authors' 2018 report gives eight items, their 2023 journal article seven (it drops the item on knowing when to trust the system), and the form on the XAITK site nine (it adds an item on reliability), with a note that researchers may use a subset. The score measures how users judge an explanation, not whether they understood it or decide better with it, and the authors present it beside separate measures of mental models, trust and task performance.

example_use_cases.description: A research team comparing counterfactual images with saliency heatmaps (LIME and layer-wise relevance propagation) for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier gives lay participants the scale after they have predicted the classifier's decision on a set of images. It chooses which explanation to develop on prediction accuracy and uses the ratings only as a second check, so that the explanation people prefer is not assumed to be the one they understand better.

A team deciding whether causal explanations of a reinforcement-learning agent's strategy in a real-time strategy game are worth the extra modelling gives participants the scale after each explained gameplay video. It compares the causal explanations with a simpler explanation and with no explanation on four items (understanding, satisfaction, sufficient detail and completeness), and pairs the ratings with a test of whether participants can predict the agent's next action.

A lender piloting a new letter that explains which factors led to a credit refusal asks pilot applicants to complete the scale after reading either the new letter or the current one. It uses the items on sufficient detail and usefulness to decide whether to add the sentence, held back so far, that says what change would have led to approval.

limitations.description: A high rating does not show that people understand the system or decide better with it. Hase and Bansal found no evidence that participants' ratings of explanation quality predicted whether the explanations helped them predict the model, Buçinca et al. found that subjective measures did not predict performance on the real decision task, and the scale's authors note that people can feel satisfied while their understanding is piecemeal or wrong.

The published evidence for the scale is small: content-validity ratings by 35 attendees of a DARPA programme meeting, an internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) of 0.86, and eight volunteers rating good and bad explanations of everyday technologies, where the difference was large but only marginally significant. The 2018 report's mean for good explanations (42.75) exceeds what eight items scored 1 to 5 can sum to, so the form tested is unclear, and the XAITK page asks for reliability data.

There are no norms or thresholds, so a score means something only against another condition in the same study, such as the current explanation or no explanation. A mean rating reported on its own, such as 4 out of 5, cannot support a claim that an explanation is satisfactory.

Versions with seven, eight and nine items are in circulation, item wording differs between them, and the form invites researchers to use a subset; Madumal et al., for example, report four items. Scores from different studies are therefore not comparable unless the same items and wording were used, and each study should report exactly which it used.

resources.abstract: The question addressed in this paper is: If we present to a user an AI system that explains how it works, how do we know whether the explanation works and the user has achieved a pragmatic understanding of the AI? In other words, how do we know that an explanainable AI system (XAI) is any good? Our focus is on the key concepts of measurement. We discuss specific methods for evaluating: (1) the goodness of explanations, (2) whether users are satisfied by explanations, (3) how well users understand the AI systems, (4) how curiosity motivates the search for explanations, (5) whether the user's trust and reliance on the AI are appropriate, and finally, (6) how the human-XAI work system performs. The recommendations we present derive from our integration of extensive research literatures and our own psychometric evaluations.

techniques.name: Forward Simulation Test
techniques.description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team must choose between feature-attribution bar charts and a short rule list as the explanation shown to credit analysts for a loan-default model. It runs a forward simulation test with 30 credit analysts on past applications, balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions, and adopts the rule list only if its gain over the no-explanation baseline is clearly larger than that of the bar charts; otherwise it treats the two as equal.

An online platform's trust and safety team uses the counterfactual variant to test whether moderators who see which words a toxicity classifier weighted can predict whether it will still flag a comment after one of those words is replaced. A score no better than the baseline tells the team that the highlights do not show how the classifier responds to edits, before it writes moderation guidance that relies on them.

A research team choosing between counterfactual images and saliency heatmaps for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier shows each group of participants explained example images, then asks them to predict the classifier's decision on 12 other images, three from each cell of its confusion matrix, without explanations. It takes forward to a study with clinicians the explanation whose group predicts best, measured against a group that saw the examples without explanations.

A local authority plans to show caseworkers, who are outside the team that built it, the reasons behind a housing-benefit fraud-risk score. Before releasing the reasons in that form, it runs a forward simulation test with caseworkers on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, using the reasons exactly as they will appear, and revises them if caseworkers who studied them predict the flag no better than caseworkers who did not.

limitations.description: A pass shows that people can anticipate the model, not that they decide better with it. Buçinca et al. found that results on a task of predicting an AI's decisions did not predict results on the real decision task, and Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. found that people who could better simulate a simple, clear model did not follow it more when that helped, and in some experiments were less able to correct its large mistakes. A claim about decisions needs a decision study.

The test is easily made trivial. If the explained examples are reused as test items, explanations that show the predicted class or a probability give the answer away, and if the model is mostly right, participants can score well by predicting the true label. Hase and Bansal found earlier studies that reused the same items for explanation and prediction; results from such designs overstate what the explanation conveys.

Effects are often small against the variation between people and items. With 32 trained undergraduates and about 180 to 320 responses per condition, Hase and Bansal's 95% confidence intervals on the change in accuracy were about 8 to 13 percentage points either side, and only LIME on tabular data clearly improved both forward and counterfactual simulation. A study must be sized for the difference it needs to detect, with a bootstrap over both participants and items.

The score holds for the people tested. Many studies use students or crowd workers because domain experts are costly to recruit, which Doshi-Velez and Kim give as the reason this kind of evaluation is cheaper; a result from lay participants does not show that the clinicians, analysts or caseworkers who will use the explanation can predict the model.

The before-and-after design credits any gain to the explanations, but participants see the same examples and test items twice, and Hase and Bansal had no group that repeated both phases without explanations, so a practice gain is not ruled out. Their participants also found it hard to remember the explained examples while predicting, so the number of examples and the time allowed must be fixed and reported when methods are compared.

resources.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.abstract: As machine learning systems become ubiquitous, there has been a surge of interest in interpretable machine learning: systems that provide explanation for their outputs. These explanations are often used to qualitatively assess other criteria such as safety or non-discrimination. However, despite the interest in interpretability, there is very little consensus on what interpretable machine learning is and how it should be measured. In this position paper, we first define interpretability and describe when interpretability is needed (and when it is not). Next, we suggest a taxonomy for rigorous evaluation and expose open questions towards a more rigorous science of interpretable machine learning.

techniques.name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
techniques.description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a nurse-facing explanation for a patient deterioration score runs think-aloud sessions with six ward nurses on a clickable prototype using past patient records. It finds that nurses read a factor that lowered the score as a sign that the patient was improving, relabels the chart, and re-tests the new labels in a second round before fixing the design for a quantitative evaluation.

The developer of a vocal emotion-recognition app that highlights which parts of a recording drove each prediction runs remote think-aloud sessions with a dozen users. One participant reads the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone of voice, a misreading that no rating of the explanation would have revealed, and the team changes how the highlight is drawn.

A bank's model risk team preparing to give loan officers counterfactual explanations (for example, the income at which a refused application would have been approved) runs think-aloud sessions with five officers on past applications, including some the model got wrong. It learns which suggestions officers would pass on to applicants and which they reject as implausible, and decides whether to filter the suggestions before release.

limitations.description: How participants are asked to talk changes what is observed. A meta-analysis of 94 studies by Fox, Ericsson and Best found that plain thinking aloud left accuracy unchanged, but that asking people to explain or describe their thinking changed performance, and that verbal reports of every kind tended to make tasks take longer. Facilitators must avoid 'why' prompts, and task times from these sessions cannot serve as performance measures.

Talking through a task can make people attend to an explanation more than they would at work. In Buçinca et al.'s think-aloud study, participants' preferences between two explanation types matched the results of a proxy task rather than those of the realistic task, and the authors suggest thinking aloud pushed people into analytical thinking, so these sessions may overstate how closely users read explanations in normal use.

Studies use few participants (between 4 and 14 in the sources for this record), so a finding shows that a problem exists, not how common it is, and cannot support a claim about the share of users who understand an explanation or about decision quality. The sessions also show only the situations their tasks include: tasks need some wrong model outputs if the team wants to see how people use an explanation when the model errs.

Not everything people do with an explanation gets said. Quick, perceptual uses leave little trace: in Zhang and Lim's study, participants called the audio examples intuitive but did not say why they found them simple. People also tend to say what they think the right answer is, the social desirability bias the GOV.UK guidance warns of. Silence about part of an explanation does not mean it went unused or was understood, and a screen recording or gaze data is needed to tell these apart.

Findings depend on the analyst: coding transcripts into themes is interpretive, so a study meant to support an assurance claim needs a stated coding scheme and a second coder. The voice and screen recordings are personal data that need participants' consent and controlled storage, and recordings made on real cases may also hold personal data about the people those cases concern.
